big: Every listed company can be lined up from biggest to smallest. Where a company stands in that line decides what kind of fund can hold it, and how bumpy the ride is likely to be.

lines: My friend says small caps gave the highest return. I want to put everything there.
Fair question. First see how the market sorts companies, then what that does to the ride.

alt: Bars of company size from biggest to smallest, cut into large, mid and small caps
caps: AMFI lines up every listed company by market value, biggest first.
The first 100 are large caps. Ranks 101 to 250 are mid caps. Everyone after is a small cap.
Prices move, so companies move. A large cap whose price falls can slip into the mid bucket.
Nobody sold anything. The label changed, and so did what the fund holds.

alt: Three lines for large, mid and small caps over ten years with the deepest fall of each marked
caps: These paths are made up to show a pattern, not real data.
Smaller companies swing harder, up and down.
Small caps ended highest here, and had the deepest fall: about 48%. Large caps fell about 8%.

alt: Three bars showing the minimum a large, mid and small cap fund must hold
caps: A large cap fund must keep at least 80% in large caps.
Mid and small cap funds must keep at least 65% in their own bucket.
The striped part is the manager's choice.

q: A company ranked 99th by market value falls in price and slips to rank 108 in the next AMFI list. A large cap fund holds it. What happens?
opts: The fund must sell the shares the same day it slips below rank 100
The company is now a mid cap, and the fund's mix shifts without a trade
The fund house has to refund investors for that change of bucket
Nothing changes in the mix, because the label stays fixed for ten years
why: No same-day sale is required. The rules are about the fund's overall mix, which is checked against the published lists.
Buckets follow rank, so the stock moves down a bucket. The fund's large cap share falls even though the manager did nothing.
There is no payment to investors. A change of bucket is part of normal market movement and the fund is not at fault.
Lists are reset every six months, not ten years. A company's bucket can change at each update.

q: A client says small caps gave the highest return, so everything should go there. What is the fair reply?
opts: Small caps have the highest ceiling and the deepest falls, so size them to survive a bad year
Agree, because the highest return so far is the best guide to the next ten years
Move everything to large caps, since small caps are not allowed for a client like him
Split it equally across twenty small cap funds, which takes away the risk of a fall
why: It states the trade honestly: more upside, deeper falls, and a size small enough that he will not sell in a panic.
Past returns say little about the next decade. The same path that gave a high return also had the deepest fall.
There is no rule against small caps for him. The question is how much of his money, not whether to own them.
Twenty funds in the same bucket still fall together, because they hold many of the same kind of company.

q: What is the minimum a large cap fund must hold in large cap stocks?
why: Half is too low to call a fund large cap. Half could sit in mid and small companies instead.
65% is the minimum for mid cap and small cap funds in their own bucket. Large cap funds have a higher bar.
SEBI sets the floor for large cap funds at 80%, and the manager chooses where the other 20% goes.
The rule is a minimum, not a full requirement. A large cap fund may hold up to 20% outside the large cap bucket.

q: In the made-up paths, small caps ended with the most money. What else did the small cap path show?
opts: It also had the deepest fall, about 48% from a peak
It never fell below its starting value of ₹100 along the way
It fell by less than the large caps in every single year
It grew by exactly the same amount in every single year
why: The path that rose the most also dropped the most. That is why the bucket must match the client's time and nerves.
The line dips well below earlier peaks, and a fall like that can leave an investor under water for years.
Large caps fell about 8% at worst here. Small caps swung much more, in both directions.
Growth was uneven, with big jumps and big drops. Smooth growth is not what smaller companies deliver.

pts: Large is rank 1 to 100, mid 101 to 250, small 251 on. Companies move between them.
Large cap funds hold at least 80% large caps. Mid and small cap funds hold at least 65% in their own bucket.
Smaller means a higher ceiling and deeper falls. Size it to the client's horizon and nerves.
